themes.note: Friday is two unrelated events and the second one is the larger. The Duo reaches shops on the 23rd in the US and more than seventy countries, with 28 more on the 30th, now under a two-unit purchase limit — which has already answered the demand question and turned Friday into a read on supply. Then Moody's reviews France, rated Aa3 negative, with the ten-year above 5% for the first time since 2002 and a Yellow Vests march in Paris on Saturday. A one-notch cut takes France to A1. Two consecutive sessions have now shown US yields ignoring French deterioration, so the honest expectation is that a downgrade does nothing here either — but a downgrade is a different kind of event from a protest, and it is the cleanest test the thesis will get.

world.title: The diesel squeeze eased from two directions at once
world.note: Tuesday's brief argued the damage had moved from crude to refined product. Wednesday pushed back on that from two sides in one session. First the inventories: distillate stocks rose 1.68m barrels to 104.3m against an expected 1.16m fall — a surprise of 2.8m barrels on the one product that has actually been squeezed, with refinery utilisation at 93.4% and crude runs up 34,000 barrels a day. Then the geopolitics: Russia agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine, possibly as early as November. BOK Financial's Dennis Kissler said a deal could unlock the tight global diesel supplies. That is the first credible route to easing the product shortage that does not require the Gulf to calm down.

Roth Capital reiterated Buy with a $235 target, citing a 50-60% uplift in deal value from Okta for AI Agents and stronger partner engagement. RBC Capital estimates customer spend could rise 25-40% from early adoption. A wave of firms — Macquarie, Scotiabank, BMO, Truist, Stephens, Baird and Oppenheimer — raised targets into roughly the $227-245 range, so the consensus average below is stale and about to move up.
20 OctRose 2.15% to 194.02, closing 5.7% above a 183.60 low on an eleven-dollar range, on a day the Nasdaq did not move. Okta's Ric Smith argued at TechCrunch Disrupt that application-level permissions cannot secure AI agents.
16 OctFell 10.20% to 187.26 — a fifth consecutive losing session and still the largest single-session fall of the position's life. It opened at 209.60, ran to 212.00 and fell to 184.89 before closing. No company news; it was named with Palantir, Datadog, Zscaler and Elastic in a broad software sell-off. Scotiabank's survey had found only 10% of customers with AI-agent contracts and revenue forecast to start in fiscal 2028 — which is the claim Wednesday's standard and target raises are arguing against.

Street: Moderate Buy · 44 analysts, average target $200.72 — 3.8% below the 208.64 close. The stock has run past the average, which is not a sell signal but does mean the laggards in the coverage have to move for the consensus to catch up.

AMZN · 262.37 · next catalyst Q3 earnings, 29 Oct

21 OctFell 0.10% to 262.37, the only faller in this book, with a low of 259.29. No company news. It went down with Alphabet on Pichai's cloud comment — Microsoft slipped too — while the rest of technology rose, which is the cloud complex being repriced for the cost of capacity rather than for demand. That is a question the 29 October print has to answer directly.
20 OctAmazon committed more than €16bn — about $18bn — to Germany for 2027, including €4.8bn to expand AWS around Frankfurt. Announced at the German government's Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin, it exceeds the €15bn it invested there in 2025. The package also covers Amazon Leo satellite broadband, a second robotics and AI research lab in Berlin, logistics upgrades running to 2028 and more than fifteen new German Prime Video productions; projects at Zweibrücken and Könnern are expected to create over 3,000 jobs. The stock moved 0.07% on it.
19 OctRose 4.98% to 262.45, its largest single-session gain of the position. It opened at 255.25, made its low at 255.22 in the first minutes and ran to 263.72. No company news — it was bought back with the AI and retail complex.
1 SepThe litigation to keep in view: the FTC and 22 state attorneys general sued over sponsored-product ad auctions. The complaint alleges Amazon changed the auction rules in 2019 and interfered in as many as 80% of sponsored-product auctions, extracting more than $20bn from over a million sellers. Advertising is $19.8bn a quarter, up 26%.

Street: Strong Buy · 60 analysts, average target $331.20 — 26.2% above the 262.37 close.

A market will fund negative free cash flow if revenue grows 26%

1. Meta held its capital-expenditure guidance, raised the floor of it, and was rewarded — on negative free cash flow. Revenue $64.60bn, up 26% against a $63.2bn consensus; advertising $63.06bn, up 26%, with impressions +10% and price per ad +14%; Family daily active people 3.64bn, up 3%. The 2026 capex range went from $130-145bn to $135-145bn and Q4 revenue was guided to $73-76bn. Q3 capex was $34.91bn against operating cash flow of $32.79bn, so free cash flow was minus $2.12bn — and the shares rose about 3% after hours. The headline profit is noise: a $9.89bn litigation charge, part of a settlement with 52 US state attorneys general over youth mental health worth up to $18.59bn, cut the operating margin from 40% to 20% and EPS to $3.83 from $7.40 excluding it. Meta also unveiled a non-voting Class C stock, effectively a two-for-one split due in January, which funds AI without diluting control.

2. And that is the read-through to the 28th, so it is worth being precise about what was and was not answered. What was answered: a company can raise AI spending, print negative free cash flow and be bought, provided the revenue line grows at 26%. What was not: whether that holds for a company whose revenue grows more slowly. Alphabet reports $195-205bn of capex on 28 October, the same afternoon the Fed decides — and on Wednesday Sundar Pichai said Google Cloud is forgoing short-term revenue to make compute trade-offs for frontier AI, with DeepMind's capacity non-negotiable and new capacity customers for next year incredibly difficult. Meta's answer was spend plus growth. Alphabet has just pre-announced spend minus growth. Alphabet fell 1.62% on a day the semiconductor index rose 1.97%, which is the market doing that arithmetic in public.

3. France crossed five percent and the American long end did not move. The ten-year OAT rose above 5% for the first time since 2002, with the 2027 budget still unresolved in a divided parliament, Carrefour down nearly 14% on riot damage, a Yellow Vests march called in Paris for Saturday and Moody's reviewing the Aa3 negative rating on Friday. The US thirty-year closed unchanged at 5.42% and a $13bn twenty-year auction cleared 0.9bp above when-issued with 31.6% going to direct bidders. Monday's reading of this — that French domestic politics was setting the price of American debt — has now failed twice in a row, on consecutive days when France got materially worse. The global-debt channel is real as a thesis; it is not operating as a daily correlation, and this brief should stop looking for it there.

The diesel squeeze eased from two directions at once

Tuesday's brief argued the damage had moved from crude to refined product. Wednesday pushed back on that from two sides in one session. First the inventories: distillate stocks rose 1.68m barrels to 104.3m against an expected 1.16m fall — a surprise of 2.8m barrels on the one product that has actually been squeezed, with refinery utilisation at 93.4% and crude runs up 34,000 barrels a day. Then the geopolitics: Russia agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine, possibly as early as November. BOK Financial's Dennis Kissler said a deal could unlock the tight global diesel supplies. That is the first credible route to easing the product shortage that does not require the Gulf to calm down.

The crude side went the other way and the price still fell. Crude stocks fell 3.06m barrels to 412.5m against an expected 820,000-barrel draw, and gasoline fell 2.95m to 205.3m against an expected 443,000 — both bullish, both larger than forecast. Cushing rose 987,000 and net crude imports rose 837,000 barrels a day. Against a draw more than three times the forecast, WTI settled $97.15, down 67 cents, having touched $100 intraday, and Brent settled $108.82, up three cents after giving up more than two dollars of gains. A market that ignores a bullish inventory print is a market pricing something else, and what it is pricing is the possibility of peace in Ukraine.

Iran hardened, and that is the other half of the session. President Masoud Pezeshkian said Washington cannot expect dialogue while blockading and threatening Iran; foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said Iran is fully prepared to defend itself. Tuesday's three-dollar reversal had rested entirely on a mediation meeting with Pakistan's army chief; twenty-four hours later the Iranian position is that there is nothing to mediate. So the diplomatic premium that took crude down on Tuesday was withdrawn on Wednesday, and crude fell anyway — which tells you the Ukraine headline is doing more work than the Iran one.

And the attacks widened geographically. Kpler counts at least 18 attacks on vessels over the past fortnight, and Kissler pointed to at least two more ships struck overnight in the Strait of Hormuz. LSEG analysts say Iran is now targeting tankers beyond the Strait, into the Gulf of Oman — which matters because the Gulf of Oman is the open-water side of the chokepoint, the stretch that re-routing was supposed to make safe. A campaign that reaches past the narrows is a campaign against the detour, and it is the reason crude flows can sit at four-fifths of pre-war levels while insurance and freight keep climbing.

weekly.headline: The worst week since June for the Nasdaq — and the Dow was the only index that rose
weekly.standfirst: Two hot inflation prints and the long end fell through both of them. September CPI came in +0.6% on the month and +3.7% on the year and September PPI at +1.3% against +0.5% expected — yet the ten-year finished the week about 14 basis points lower and the thirty-year 17 lower at 5.43%, with hike odds for 28 October ending near 27% after touching 50%. The explanation is the retail sales control group at +0.1% against +0.3% expected: gasoline did over half of CPI, rose 20.3% at the producer level and supplied most of the retail beat, so the market read it as a tax on demand. The Nasdaq fell 4.5% and the S&P 1.9%, both their worst week since June; the Russell fell 3% at three weekly sigma; and the Dow rose 0.7%, the only index up. Crude broke $100, from $90.76 to $101.41, through roughly 37m barrels of announced emergency release. In the book OKTA fell 19.3% and PLTR 11.0%, both on no company news, with PLTR trading to 184.45 — within a cent of the entry. AAPL rose 2.0% after the iPhone Duo sold out within moments of pre-orders opening. The week cost -98.36. Heat 3.00R against 3.0R, unchanged since 14 September.

Four of six instruments had a move of more than one weekly sigma, and the ranking is the whole week. The Russell fell 3.05% at 3.17σ — the largest weekly reading on this board in the series. The Nasdaq fell 4.48% at 1.99σ, crude rose 11.73% at 1.85σ and the S&P fell 1.95% at 1.69σ. And then the two that did nothing: the Dow rose 0.67% at 0.63σ and gold fell 0.20% at 0.13σ. A week in which the small-cap index has its most unusual move of the series, the Nasdaq has its worst week since June, crude rises eleven percent and gold does not move at all is not a week with one story in it.

The indices, precisely. Across the five sessions the S&P fell 152.10 points, or 1.9%, to 7,659.44; the Nasdaq 1,226.14, or 4.5%, to 26,140.03 — its worst week since June, as was the S&P's; the Russell 85.61, or 3%, to 2,721.37. The Dow rose 347.46 points, or 0.7%, to 52,002.41, and was the only index up. For the year the S&P is now up 11.9%, the Nasdaq 12.5%, the Russell 9.6% and the Dow 8.2% — the Dow has closed almost the whole of the gap the Nasdaq built over the first nine months.

Two first-tier prints, both hot, and the long end fell anyway. September CPI on Wednesday came in +0.6% on the month and +3.7% on the year, core +0.3% and +2.6%, both above forecast — with gasoline +9.1% and +34.2% doing over half the monthly increase on the BLS's own reckoning, and shelter and core services both accelerating to +0.4%. September PPI on Thursday came in at +1.3% against +0.5% expected, +6.3% on the year, with energy goods +10.8% and gasoline +20.3% at the producer level. Hike odds for 28 October went from about 22% to roughly 50% to about 27% inside three sessions. And the ten-year finished the week about 14 basis points lower and the thirty-year about 17, at 5.43%. Fed Chair Warsh's IMF remarks left roughly an 85% hold priced for this month.

The number that explains it is in the retail sales report, not the inflation ones. Headline retail sales rose 0.8% against 0.3% expected, to $745.0bn. But the control group rose only 0.1% against 0.3% expected, and excluding petrol stations the increase was 0.2%. So the consumer is not spending more; the consumer is paying more for fuel. Gasoline did over half of CPI, rose a fifth at the producer level, and supplied most of the retail beat. The bond market read that as a tax on demand rather than inflation to be met with hikes, and bought duration into two hot prints. That is the single most important thing the week established.

And crude broke a hundred dollars. WTI went from $90.76 to $101.41, +11.7%, and Brent from $103.35 to $109.86, touching $110 on Friday for the first time since May. Gold finished the week almost exactly where it started, at $4,166.39, having fallen 1.34% on the CPI and risen 1.60% on the PPI. An eleven-percent week in oil and a flat week in gold is a market pricing a supply problem, not a monetary one.

OKTA is the week. It fell 19.3% across five consecutive losing sessions, from 232.13 to 187.26, taking −44.87 out of the book — more than half the week's loss on its own. On Monday it opened at 235.00, a 52-week high; by Friday it had fallen 10.20% in a single session, the largest of its life. The position has gone from +2.46R to +0.23R. PLTR gave back everything, and AAPL was the only thing that worked. Palantir fell 11.0% from the all-time closing high of 209.05 it set on 9 October, and on Friday traded down to 184.45 — within a cent of the entry — before closing at +0.08R. The entire Goldman-and-Barclays re-rating of 9 October has been returned, on no company news. Against that, AAPL rose 2.0% in a week the Nasdaq fell 4.5%, and at +1.08R it is one of only 2 positions above +1R — settled on Friday by the iPhone Duo selling out within moments of pre-orders opening, with shipping slipping to late January 2027 on some configurations and resale at up to $5,000 against a $1,999 list.

AMZN is now 79% of the open profit, and that is the book's real exposure. It fell 4.7% across the week, from 262.43 to 250.00, costing −37.29 — and still accounts for 79% of the +131.02 held open, at +5.17R. That share rose over a week in which the position lost money, because everything else lost more. Its stop sits at the fill, which protects every dollar of capital and none of the gain, and after a week like this one that is the only decision still outstanding in this book.

Where the quarter stands · twelve sessions in

Q4 is +131.02 at +6.55R, of which none is realised: it is open profit accrued since entry, not a Q4 return. Q3 finished at +17.04, +0.84R, against the S&P's +2.0%. On $1,335.73 of capital still committed the open book is +9.81% since entry. The week cost -98.36 against an S&P down 1.9%, a Nasdaq down 4.5% and a Dow up 0.7%, which is the comparison that matters: 2 of the 4 positions are above +1R (AAPL at +1.08R, AMZN at +5.17R), and the index this book owns nothing in was the only one that rose.

Two hot prints, a bank fine, a foldable sell-out, and a rotation that completed

1. The long end fell through two hot inflation prints, and that settles a three-week argument. The thesis built from 29 September was that the long end was rising on supply and global debt rather than inflation. This week tested it to destruction: the ten-year spiked to 5.33% on the CPI and closed back at 5.19%; then fell 12 basis points on the PPI to a three-week low; and finished the week about 14 basis points lower, with the thirty-year 17 lower at 5.43%. Neither explanation survives. An inflation trade would have risen and stayed risen. A pure supply trade would not have spiked on CPI at all. What fits is the retail sales control group at +0.1%: the market read energy-driven price rises as demand destruction and bought duration into them. Hike odds for 28 October ended the week near 27% after touching 50%.

2. The banks reported and the split told you where the cycle is. JPMorgan missed for the first time in nearly three years — $5.57 against $5.93 expected — on investment banking and a fixed-income desk that slowed from the summer. Goldman earned $17.01 against $12.25 a year ago on stock trading, with bond trading slower. Citigroup's profit rose 40% but card profits were flat. Bank of America missed on Wednesday — $0.91 a share including a charge, $1.08 against $1.10 excluding it, revenue $30bn against $30.58bn, investment banking fees −11% and sales and trading −5% — the day after the Treasury fined it $1.2bn, the third-largest penalty in that department's history, for willful Bank Secrecy Act violations involving more than $5bn of suspicious transactions. The pattern: equity desks busy, bond desks quiet, consumer flat.

3. Apple's foldable sold out in minutes, which was the only checkable fact in a fortnight of sourcing. Three parties had disagreed from anonymous supply-chain contacts — Nikkei on iPhone 18 Pro cuts, Securities Times on Duo orders raised 30% toward ten million units, Bank of America on shorter Pro delivery times — and Friday replaced all of it with evidence. Pre-orders opened at 8am Eastern, stock went within moments, shipping slipped to late January 2027 on some configurations, Apple called demand nothing short of extraordinary, and units resold at up to $5,000 against a $1,999 list. The fair caveat is that a sell-out is a ratio and Apple probably built few of them. The resale premium is harder to argue with.

4. And the rotation completed, which is the week's real lesson for this book. Over five sessions the Dow rose 0.7% and was the only index up, while the Nasdaq fell 4.5% and the Russell 3%. Friday's sell-off is the one to study: the Nasdaq fell 2.15% and the Dow 0.34% while the ten-year rose two basis points. That was not a rate event. Micron fell 5.6% and Intel 5.8% as investors grew more concerned about how long AI infrastructure spending will last, and Okta, Palantir, Datadog, Zscaler and Elastic were sold together. A rate scare reverses when the Fed is repriced — and it did, on Thursday. A thesis under question does not.

Crude rose eleven percent through two emergency releases

WTI went from $90.76 to $101.41 across the week, up 11.7%, and Brent touched $110 on Friday for the first time since May. It did so through four separate supply events and against the two largest tools short of policy that the agencies have. Monday: +3.28% on renewed Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. Tuesday: WTI up, Brent down, as traders weighed a possible US–Russia diesel deal against escalation in Yemen. Wednesday: +1.01% after a Houthi missile hit an office tower at Aramco's Dhahran headquarters — top three floors damaged, limited fire, no injuries, a command centre rather than a producing asset. Thursday: +3.03% on a US inventory draw. Friday: +3.51%.

Friday's reasons are worth separating because one of them is new. A Saudi-led coalition intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at Yanbu — the Red Sea export terminal whose entire strategic value is that crude leaving from it bypasses the Strait of Hormuz. Targeting the hedge against the chokepoint is an escalation in kind, not degree. Ukrainian strikes also damaged the Ryazan refinery, shutting a primary crude unit, which bears directly on Russian diesel. And the EIA reported US crude stocks down 8.6m barrels to 415.6m, with distillates down 2.5m.

Against all of which: the IEA announced the release of over 20m barrels of emergency supply, and Washington offered up to 17m through a reserve exchange. Roughly 37m barrels of announced additional supply, and the price rose 3.5% on the day and 11.7% on the week. The reason is the number Aramco's Amin Nasser has been repeating: commercial inventory under 6 billion barrels against roughly 10 billion before the crisis, with less than 10% practically available and up to two years to rebuild. A release needs a cushion to land on. There is not one.

And the diesel number is how all of this reaches a book with no oil position in it. The IEA reported combined net gasoil exports from the Middle East and Russia down 1.3m barrels a day in September to 820,000 — more than 60% lower year on year — with no stock rebuild expected before the second half of 2027, because the binding constraint is how much Russian refining capacity is actually running. Gulf crude exports are back at 13.9m barrels a day, over 75% of pre-war; refined product exports are 1.9m against 4.7m. Crude flows and product does not. That gap is why gasoline rose 20.3% at the producer level in September and did over half of the CPI increase — and the October print, due 10 November, carries a crude price eleven percent higher than when this week began.

positions.title: What is actually happening at the companies you own

items.html: Sundar Pichai said Google Cloud is giving up revenue to feed its own AI. On the Big Technology Podcast he said the business is forgoing short-term revenues because we are making compute trade-offs to support frontier AI development, called giving DeepMind enough capacity non-negotiable, and said taking on new customers who need capacity for next year would be incredibly difficult. He put no number on it and gave no date for when added capacity reaches outside customers.

3. France crossed five percent and the American long end did not move. The ten-year OAT rose above 5% for the first time since 2002, with the 2027 budget still unresolved in a divided parliament, Carrefour down nearly 14% on riot damage, a Yellow Vests march called in Paris for Saturday and Moody's reviewing the Aa3 negative rating on Friday. The US thirty-year closed unchanged at 5.42% and a $13bn twenty-year auction cleared 0.9bp above when-issued with 31.6% going to direct bidders. Monday's reading of this — that French domestic politics was setting the price of American debt — has now failed twice in a row, on consecutive days when France got materially worse. The global-debt channel is real as a thesis; it is not operating as a daily correlation, and this brief should stop looking for it there.

The diesel squeeze eased from two directions at once

Tuesday's brief argued the damage had moved from crude to refined product. Wednesday pushed back on that from two sides in one session. First the inventories: distillate stocks rose 1.68m barrels to 104.3m against an expected 1.16m fall — a surprise of 2.8m barrels on the one product that has actually been squeezed, with refinery utilisation at 93.4% and crude runs up 34,000 barrels a day. Then the geopolitics: Russia agreed to resume US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine, possibly as early as November. BOK Financial's Dennis Kissler said a deal could unlock the tight global diesel supplies. That is the first credible route to easing the product shortage that does not require the Gulf to calm down.

The crude side went the other way and the price still fell. Crude stocks fell 3.06m barrels to 412.5m against an expected 820,000-barrel draw, and gasoline fell 2.95m to 205.3m against an expected 443,000 — both bullish, both larger than forecast. Cushing rose 987,000 and net crude imports rose 837,000 barrels a day. Against a draw more than three times the forecast, WTI settled $97.15, down 67 cents, having touched $100 intraday, and Brent settled $108.82, up three cents after giving up more than two dollars of gains. A market that ignores a bullish inventory print is a market pricing something else, and what it is pricing is the possibility of peace in Ukraine.

Iran hardened, and that is the other half of the session. President Masoud Pezeshkian said Washington cannot expect dialogue while blockading and threatening Iran; foreign minister Abbas Araqchi said Iran is fully prepared to defend itself. Tuesday's three-dollar reversal had rested entirely on a mediation meeting with Pakistan's army chief; twenty-four hours later the Iranian position is that there is nothing to mediate. So the diplomatic premium that took crude down on Tuesday was withdrawn on Wednesday, and crude fell anyway — which tells you the Ukraine headline is doing more work than the Iran one.

And the attacks widened geographically. Kpler counts at least 18 attacks on vessels over the past fortnight, and Kissler pointed to at least two more ships struck overnight in the Strait of Hormuz. LSEG analysts say Iran is now targeting tankers beyond the Strait, into the Gulf of Oman — which matters because the Gulf of Oman is the open-water side of the chokepoint, the stretch that re-routing was supposed to make safe. A campaign that reaches past the narrows is a campaign against the detour, and it is the reason crude flows can sit at four-fifths of pre-war levels while insurance and freight keep climbing.

Then Moody's reviews France, rated Aa3 negative, with the ten-year above 5% for the first time since 2002 and a Yellow Vests march in Paris on Saturday. A one-notch cut takes France to A1. Two consecutive sessions have now shown US yields ignoring French deterioration, so the honest expectation is that a downgrade does nothing here either — but a downgrade is a different kind of event from a protest, and it is the cleanest test the thesis will get.

Then the 28th, which is the day this book turns on. Alphabet reports $195-205bn of capex on the same afternoon the Fed decides. A hold is expected and December is about 94% priced for a hike. Meta has just shown that the market will fund heavy AI spending and negative free cash flow when revenue grows 26%; Pichai has just said Alphabet's cloud revenue is being held back on purpose. Those two facts point in opposite directions and they resolve on one afternoon.

Whether AAPL stays above +1R through Friday's launch, at +1.06R and 42% of the open profit. And whether GOOG can stop making lower lows into the 28th, at +0.25R and the weakest holding here. weekly.headline: The worst week since June for the Nasdaq — and the Dow was the only index that rose
weekly.standfirst: Two hot inflation prints and the long end fell through both of them. September CPI came in +0.6% on the month and +3.7% on the year and September PPI at +1.3% against +0.5% expected — yet the ten-year finished the week about 14 basis points lower and the thirty-year 17 lower at 5.43%, with hike odds for 28 October ending near 27% after touching 50%. The explanation is the retail sales control group at +0.1% against +0.3% expected: gasoline did over half of CPI, rose 20.3% at the producer level and supplied most of the retail beat, so the market read it as a tax on demand. The Nasdaq fell 4.5% and the S&P 1.9%, both their worst week since June; the Russell fell 3% at three weekly sigma; and the Dow rose 0.7%, the only index up. Crude broke $100, from $90.76 to $101.41, through roughly 37m barrels of announced emergency release. In the book OKTA fell 19.3% in five sessions on no company news, from +2.46R to +0.23R, and AMZN was stopped out on Wednesday, gapping through its breakeven stop. AAPL rose 2.0% and is the only position left above +1R, after the iPhone Duo sold out within moments of pre-orders opening. The week cost -83.62. Heat 3.05R against 3.0R, unchanged since 14 September.

Four of six instruments had a move of more than one weekly sigma, and the ranking is the whole week. The Russell fell 3.05% at 3.17σ — the largest weekly reading on this board in the series. The Nasdaq fell 4.48% at 1.99σ, crude rose 11.73% at 1.85σ and the S&P fell 1.95% at 1.69σ. And then the two that did nothing: the Dow rose 0.67% at 0.63σ and gold fell 0.20% at 0.13σ. A week in which the small-cap index has its most unusual move of the series, the Nasdaq has its worst week since June, crude rises eleven percent and gold does not move at all is not a week with one story in it.

The indices, precisely. Across the five sessions the S&P fell 152.10 points, or 1.9%, to 7,659.44; the Nasdaq 1,226.14, or 4.5%, to 26,140.03 — its worst week since June, as was the S&P's; the Russell 85.61, or 3%, to 2,721.37. The Dow rose 347.46 points, or 0.7%, to 52,002.41, and was the only index up. For the year the S&P is now up 11.9%, the Nasdaq 12.5%, the Russell 9.6% and the Dow 8.2% — the Dow has closed almost the whole of the gap the Nasdaq built over the first nine months.

Two first-tier prints, both hot, and the long end fell anyway. September CPI on Wednesday came in +0.6% on the month and +3.7% on the year, core +0.3% and +2.6%, both above forecast — with gasoline +9.1% and +34.2% doing over half the monthly increase on the BLS's own reckoning, and shelter and core services both accelerating to +0.4%. September PPI on Thursday came in at +1.3% against +0.5% expected, +6.3% on the year, with energy goods +10.8% and gasoline +20.3% at the producer level. Hike odds for 28 October went from about 22% to roughly 50% to about 27% inside three sessions. And the ten-year finished the week about 14 basis points lower and the thirty-year about 17, at 5.43%. Fed Chair Warsh's IMF remarks left roughly an 85% hold priced for this month.

The number that explains it is in the retail sales report, not the inflation ones. Headline retail sales rose 0.8% against 0.3% expected, to $745.0bn. But the control group rose only 0.1% against 0.3% expected, and excluding petrol stations the increase was 0.2%. So the consumer is not spending more; the consumer is paying more for fuel. Gasoline did over half of CPI, rose a fifth at the producer level, and supplied most of the retail beat. The bond market read that as a tax on demand rather than inflation to be met with hikes, and bought duration into two hot prints. That is the single most important thing the week established.

And crude broke a hundred dollars. WTI went from $90.76 to $101.41, +11.7%, and Brent from $103.35 to $109.86, touching $110 on Friday for the first time since May. Gold finished the week almost exactly where it started, at $4,166.39, having fallen 1.34% on the CPI and risen 1.60% on the PPI. An eleven-percent week in oil and a flat week in gold is a market pricing a supply problem, not a monetary one.

The worst week of the stretch — and the R column is the part to read

The percentage and dollar columns above are the week, 12 to 16 October. The R column is where each position stands against the risk it was opened with. The book moved -83.62 across the five sessions and now shows +37.07 open at +1.81R. One position closed: AMZN was stopped out on Wednesday the 15th, gapping through its breakeven stop at the open, realising -2.85 or -0.14R — and costing -34.62 measured from the previous Friday's close. The nearest line on the week's lows was GOOG, 8.89% above its 305.67 stop. Heat is 3.05R against a 3.0R cap (2.04R excluding the managed GOOG position) and has not moved since 14 September.

OKTA is the week. It fell 19.3% across five consecutive losing sessions, from 232.13 to 187.26, taking −44.87 out of the book — more than half the week's loss on its own. On Monday it opened at 235.00, a 52-week high; by Friday it had fallen 10.20% in a single session, the largest of its life. The position has gone from +2.46R to +0.23R. There was no company news in any of the five sessions. What there was instead: a stock up 152.4% on the year, one screen calling it 102.4% above intrinsic value, $54.8m of insider selling over twelve months, and agent revenue not forecast to begin until fiscal 2028. The 5 October valuation note has now largely been settled against the position.

AAPL was the only thing that worked, and only at the end. It rose 2.0% across the week while the Nasdaq fell 4.5%, and at +1.04R it is the only position left above +1R, carrying 58% of the open profit. The week's argument about iPhone demand ran through three contradictory supply-chain reports and was then settled on Friday by the only checkable event in it: the iPhone Duo sold out within moments of pre-orders opening, Apple called the demand nothing short of extraordinary, shipping slipped to late January 2027 on some configurations, and units resold at up to $5,000 against a $1,999 list. GOOG, meanwhile, fell 3.2% to +0.55R, its lowest close since 2 October.

And the AMZN exit is the week's lesson, stated once. The stop was at the fill, 251.84, which made the position riskless in the sense that mattered: no capital could be lost. It did not make the fill riskless. On Wednesday the stock gapped to a 250.89 open, ninety-five cents below the stop, with no trade in between — so the exit was the open, not the stop, and the trade realised -2.85 instead of nothing. It then fell to 248.65 and closed 254.76, above the stop. In a $250 stock that can gap three dollars overnight, a breakeven stop means risk of about a dollar a share, and the position most likely to be taken out is the one with the tightest line regardless of how safe that line looks. Heat did not fall when it closed, either — a stop at the entry was carrying no risk, so removing it freed none.

Where the quarter stands · twelve sessions in

Q4 is +34.22 at +1.67R, of which -2.85 is realised and the rest is open profit accrued since entry — not a Q4 return. Q3 finished at +12.31, +0.58R, against the S&P's +2.0%. On $830.56 of capital still committed the open book is +4.46% since entry. The week cost -83.62 against an S&P down 1.9%, a Nasdaq down 4.5% and a Dow up 0.7%, which is the comparison that matters: 1 of the 3 positions is above +1R (AAPL at +1.04R), and the index this book owns nothing in was the only one that rose.

Two hot prints, a bank fine, a foldable sell-out, and a rotation that completed

1. The long end fell through two hot inflation prints, and that settles a three-week argument. The thesis built from 29 September was that the long end was rising on supply and global debt rather than inflation. This week tested it to destruction: the ten-year spiked to 5.33% on the CPI and closed back at 5.19%; then fell 12 basis points on the PPI to a three-week low; and finished the week about 14 basis points lower, with the thirty-year 17 lower at 5.43%. Neither explanation survives. An inflation trade would have risen and stayed risen. A pure supply trade would not have spiked on CPI at all. What fits is the retail sales control group at +0.1%: the market read energy-driven price rises as demand destruction and bought duration into them. Hike odds for 28 October ended the week near 27% after touching 50%.

2. The banks reported and the split told you where the cycle is. JPMorgan missed for the first time in nearly three years — $5.57 against $5.93 expected — on investment banking and a fixed-income desk that slowed from the summer. Goldman earned $17.01 against $12.25 a year ago on stock trading, with bond trading slower. Citigroup's profit rose 40% but card profits were flat. Bank of America missed on Wednesday — $0.91 a share including a charge, $1.08 against $1.10 excluding it, revenue $30bn against $30.58bn, investment banking fees −11% and sales and trading −5% — the day after the Treasury fined it $1.2bn, the third-largest penalty in that department's history, for willful Bank Secrecy Act violations involving more than $5bn of suspicious transactions. The pattern: equity desks busy, bond desks quiet, consumer flat.

3. Apple's foldable sold out in minutes, which was the only checkable fact in a fortnight of sourcing. Three parties had disagreed from anonymous supply-chain contacts — Nikkei on iPhone 18 Pro cuts, Securities Times on Duo orders raised 30% toward ten million units, Bank of America on shorter Pro delivery times — and Friday replaced all of it with evidence. Pre-orders opened at 8am Eastern, stock went within moments, shipping slipped to late January 2027 on some configurations, Apple called demand nothing short of extraordinary, and units resold at up to $5,000 against a $1,999 list. The fair caveat is that a sell-out is a ratio and Apple probably built few of them. The resale premium is harder to argue with.

4. And the rotation completed, which is the week's real lesson for this book. Over five sessions the Dow rose 0.7% and was the only index up, while the Nasdaq fell 4.5% and the Russell 3%. Friday's sell-off is the one to study: the Nasdaq fell 2.15% and the Dow 0.34% while the ten-year rose two basis points. That was not a rate event. Micron fell 5.6% and Intel 5.8% as investors grew more concerned about how long AI infrastructure spending will last, and Okta, Palantir, Datadog, Zscaler and Elastic were sold together. A rate scare reverses when the Fed is repriced — and it did, on Thursday. A thesis under question does not.

Crude rose eleven percent through two emergency releases

WTI went from $90.76 to $101.41 across the week, up 11.7%, and Brent touched $110 on Friday for the first time since May. It did so through four separate supply events and against the two largest tools short of policy that the agencies have. Monday: +3.28% on renewed Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure and tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. Tuesday: WTI up, Brent down, as traders weighed a possible US–Russia diesel deal against escalation in Yemen. Wednesday: +1.01% after a Houthi missile hit an office tower at Aramco's Dhahran headquarters — top three floors damaged, limited fire, no injuries, a command centre rather than a producing asset. Thursday: +3.03% on a US inventory draw. Friday: +3.51%.

Friday's reasons are worth separating because one of them is new. A Saudi-led coalition intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at Yanbu — the Red Sea export terminal whose entire strategic value is that crude leaving from it bypasses the Strait of Hormuz. Targeting the hedge against the chokepoint is an escalation in kind, not degree. Ukrainian strikes also damaged the Ryazan refinery, shutting a primary crude unit, which bears directly on Russian diesel. And the EIA reported US crude stocks down 8.6m barrels to 415.6m, with distillates down 2.5m.

Against all of which: the IEA announced the release of over 20m barrels of emergency supply, and Washington offered up to 17m through a reserve exchange. Roughly 37m barrels of announced additional supply, and the price rose 3.5% on the day and 11.7% on the week. The reason is the number Aramco's Amin Nasser has been repeating: commercial inventory under 6 billion barrels against roughly 10 billion before the crisis, with less than 10% practically available and up to two years to rebuild. A release needs a cushion to land on. There is not one.

And the diesel number is how all of this reaches a book with no oil position in it. The IEA reported combined net gasoil exports from the Middle East and Russia down 1.3m barrels a day in September to 820,000 — more than 60% lower year on year — with no stock rebuild expected before the second half of 2027, because the binding constraint is how much Russian refining capacity is actually running. Gulf crude exports are back at 13.9m barrels a day, over 75% of pre-war; refined product exports are 1.9m against 4.7m. Crude flows and product does not. That gap is why gasoline rose 20.3% at the producer level in September and did over half of the CPI increase — and the October print, due 10 November, carries a crude price eleven percent higher than when this week began.

Ten days of empty calendar, then four events in three days

There is nothing dated for ten days, and that has not been true since late September. No print, no earnings, no scheduled event from any company held, until the Duo ships on Friday 23 October. Then the calendar compresses: the Fed and Alphabet on Wednesday the 28th, Apple and Amazon on Thursday the 29th, Palantir on 2 November and October CPI on the 10th. Four of the five positions this book has held during October report inside those three days.

Alphabet on the 28th is the one that has changed character. A fortnight ago its $195-205bn of capex and the 3.6-gigawatt Constellation deal were the bull case — evidence of scale. After a Friday in which Micron fell 5.6% and Intel 5.8% because investors are no longer sure how long AI infrastructure spending lasts, the same number is the thing the print has to defend. And it lands the same afternoon the Fed decides, so two factors resolve on one day for a book exposed to both.

What to watch in this book. Whether AAPL holds what the pre-order gave it — at +1.04R it is the only position above +1R and carries 58% of the open profit, a concentration that arrived by subtraction. Whether OKTA finds a floor at +0.23R after nineteen percent in five sessions. And whether GOOG can hold 335 into its own print. All of them now turn on one question, and it is no longer the Fed: whether the market still believes the AI build.

The standing position: do nothing, because nothing can be done. Heat is 3.05R against a 3.0R cap and has not moved in twenty-seven sessions, so no position can be added however attractive anything looks. This week was the first real test of that constraint: two holdings fell more than ten percent, one closed, and the book could not respond to any of it. The ten days to the 23rd are the first stretch since September with nothing to react to, which makes them the right time to decide what this book should look like when it can act again.
